TUOL SLENG, Cambodia (CNN)  -- The trial of a former prison chief with the Khmer Rouge movement resumed inside a packed Cambodian courtroom Monday, with prosecutors painting a grim picture of inmates who were electrocuted, whipped and beaten to death. Duch ran a prison where people were tortured and killed under the Khmer Rouge. Kaing Guek Eav, a former math teacher and a born-again Christian, displayed no emotion as the U.N.-backed tribunal accused him not just of overseeing the torture and killing of more than 15,000 men, women and children three decades ago -- but of actively taking part in some of them. The trial of the 66-year-old man, better known as Duch, resumed Monday just outside the Cambodian capital, Phnom Penh. Spectators, many of them survivors of the abuse, watched the proceedings from an auditorium separated from the courtroom by a large glass window. The proceedings began with Duch offering a basic introduction of himself. Court officials then read out the findings of their lengthy investigation. Prosecutors contend Duch ran S-21, a prison that had been converted from a school. Here, men, women and children were shackled to iron beds and tortured -- before they were beaten to death, prosecutors said. Many of the victims were military officials or Communist Party members targeted for not going along with the philosophy of the ultra-Maoist Khmer Rouge movement, prosecutors said. Duch faces charges that include crimes against humanity, war crimes, torture and murder. He has admitted his role in the Khmer Rouge's genocidal reign.  Watch why his trial is significant » . The movement swept to power in 1975. Three years, eight months and 20 days later, at least 1.7 million people -- nearly one-quarter of Cambodia's population -- were dead from execution, disease, starvation and overwork, according to the Documentation Center of Cambodia. The non-profit organization has been at the forefront of recording the atrocities committed during the Khmer Rouge regime. S-21 was one of 189 similar institutions across Cambodia. Duch is the first former Khmer Rouge leader to stand trial. The tribunal, which is made up of Cambodian and international judges, does not have the power to impose the death penalty. If convicted, Duch faces from five years to life in prison. The trial is expected to last three or four months. "Probably the most important thing about this court is: even after 35 years, you are still not going to get away with it. That is the message," said Chief Prosecutor Robert Petit. Even though Duch was not a senior leader with the movement, many Cambodians were relieved that one of the regime's former leaders was facing justice, said Youk Chhang, head of the Documentation Center of Cambodia. "I think there is a feeling of, well you know, finally -- now it's finally happening after all these years of waiting -- hearing, fighting, negotiating," he told CNN last month. "People have that kind of sense of relief that it's now moving. When I ask people around the center today, people say, 'Oh, it's about time.'" Four of the regime's former leaders, also accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity, await trial before the tribunal. The regime's leader, Pol Pot, died in 1998. "It all seems so fresh," said Norng Champhal, who was a starving little boy when Vietnamese forces invaded the prison. He was separated from his mother after a night in the prison and never saw her again. "It's hard to control my feelings when I see this," he said, as he watched footage of the prison taken 30 years ago. "I wonder whether my parents were tortured like these people," he said. CNN's Dan Rivers contributed to this report.

# The Trial of Duch: Confronting Cambodia's Dark Past

The trial of Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary alias Duch, resumed in Cambodia as the country continued its long-delayed reckoning with the atrocities committed under the Khmer Rouge regime. Duch stands accused of serving as the chief architect of torture and mass killing at one of the regime's most notorious detention facilities, and his case represents a pivotal moment in Cambodia's pursuit of justice for crimes that occurred more than three decades ago.

Prosecutors have presented a damning case against Duch, alleging that his role extended far beyond mere administrative oversight. According to the charges, he did not simply supervise the systematic brutality inflicted upon prisoners—he actively participated in the torture and execution of victims himself. In total, prosecutors contend that Duch bears responsibility for the deaths of more than 15,000 men, women, and children, a staggering toll that underscores the scale of suffering inflicted under his command.

At the center of these allegations is S-21, formerly known as Tuol Sleng, a facility that had once served as a secondary school before being repurposed by the Khmer Rouge into a center for interrogation, torture, and execution. Under Duch's leadership, prisoners held at S-21 were shackled in cramped conditions, subjected to brutal torture designed to extract confessions, and ultimately beaten to death once they had outlived their usefulness to the regime. The facility became emblematic of the Khmer Rouge's machinery of terror, a place where ordinary structures of education were transformed into instruments of extermination.

The victims who passed through S-21 were often not random targets but individuals specifically identified as threats to the regime's rigid ideological purity. Many were military officials or members of the Communist Party itself, accused of harboring disloyalty or failing to fully embrace the extreme vision of agrarian communism that defined Khmer Rouge doctrine. This pattern reveals the paranoid, self-devouring nature of the regime, which turned its violence not only against perceived external enemies but against its own ranks in relentless purges.

These horrors unfolded within the broader context of the Khmer Rouge's rule, which began in 1975 and persisted for nearly four years before its collapse. During this brief but catastrophic period, the regime's policies resulted in the deaths of at least 1.7 million people—approximately one-quarter of Cambodia's entire population at the time. Deaths came not only through direct execution but also through the devastating combination of disease, starvation, and forced labor imposed upon a population subjected to radical social engineering. The trial of Duch thus stands as a small but significant step toward addressing one of the twentieth century's most devastating humanitarian catastrophes, offering survivors and the international community alike a measure of accountability for crimes that reshaped an entire nation.

# Cambodia's Khmer Rouge Tribunal Resumes Trial of Notorious Prison Chief

The United Nations-backed tribunal in Cambodia resumed proceedings this week in the trial of Kaing Guek Eav, better known by his revolutionary alias "Duch," who served as the chief administrator of the infamous S-21 prison during the brutal reign of the Khmer Rouge. Prosecutors allege that under Duch's direct supervision, more than 15,000 men, women, and children were systematically tortured, interrogated, and ultimately executed at the facility, which was housed in a former high school in Phnom Penh known as Tuol Sleng.

The reconvening of the tribunal represents a critical milestone in Cambodia's long and often fraught journey toward justice for the crimes committed during one of the twentieth century's most devastating genocides. Between 1975 and 1979, the Khmer Rouge regime, led by Pol Pot, implemented radical policies aimed at transforming Cambodia into an agrarian utopia—policies that instead resulted in mass starvation, forced labor, and systematic executions. Historians estimate that as many as 1.7 million Cambodians, roughly a quarter of the country's population at the time, perished during this period through execution, disease, and famine.

Duch's trial holds particular significance as it represents one of the first opportunities for survivors and victims' families to see a senior Khmer Rouge official held formally accountable in a court of law. As the former head of S-21, Duch occupied a uniquely central role in the machinery of the regime's terror, personally overoso the interrogation and torture of thousands of perceived enemies of the state, many of whom were ordinary citizens swept up in the paranoid purges that characterized the era.

The tribunal, formally known as the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, was established through a joint agreement between the Cambodian government and the United Nations after years of difficult negotiations over its structure, funding, and jurisdiction. The court has faced numerous obstacles since its inception, including political interference, funding shortfalls, and lengthy delays that have tested the patience of survivors, many of whom are now elderly and eager to see justice served before their own passing.

For many Cambodians, the resumption of Duch's trial offers a rare public forum in which the horrors of the Khmer Rouge period can be formally documented, examined, and acknowledged. Survivors and witnesses have provided harrowing testimony about the conditions at S-21, describing systematic torture techniques used to extract false confessions, the overcrowded and inhumane conditions in which prisoners were held, and the ultimate fate of those who did not survive their detention—many of whom were transported to the "Killing Fields" outside Phnom Penh for execution.

As the trial proceeds, it continues to draw significant international attention, both as a mechanism for delivering justice to victims and their families and as a broader statement about the international community's commitment to holding perpetrators of mass atrocities accountable, regardless of how much time has passed since the crimes were committed. The outcome of this case is expected to set important precedents for the tribunal's subsequent prosecutions of other senior Khmer Rouge leaders still awaiting trial.

# Tuol Sleng: Cambodia's Memorial to a Dark Chapter in History

Tuol Sleng, formally known as Security Prison 21 (S-21), stands as one of Cambodia's most significant historical sites, serving as a stark reminder of the atrocities committed during the Khmer Rouge regime from 1975 to 1979. Located in Phnom Penh, this former high school was transformed by the Khmer Rouge into a detention and interrogation center where thousands of Cambodians suffered unimaginable brutality.

## From School to Prison

Before the Khmer Rouge seized power, the site functioned as Tuol Svay Prey High School. Once Pol Pot's regime took control, the buildings were repurposed into a prison facility. Classrooms were converted into cramped cells and torture chambers, and the peaceful educational environment gave way to a place of fear and suffering.

## A Site of Systematic Persecution

Under the Khmer Rouge's rule, an estimated 12,000 to 20,000 people were imprisoned at Tuol Sleng. Prisoners included perceived enemies of the regime—intellectuals, former government officials, teachers, and even Khmer Rouge cadres accused of disloyalty. The regime meticulously documented its prisoners through photographs and forced confessions, creating an extensive archive that would later serve as crucial evidence of the genocide. Tragically, only a handful of prisoners are known to have survived their imprisonment.

## The Museum Today

In 1980, the site was converted into the Tuol Sleng Genocide Museum, dedicated to preserving the memory of the victims and educating visitors about this devastating period in Cambodian history. The museum displays thousands of photographs of victims, instruments of torture, and personal accounts that offer a haunting glimpse into the horrors that unfolded within these walls.

Visitors to Tuol Sleng today walk through preserved cells, view rooms filled with photographs of the deceased, and encounter exhibits detailing the systematic cruelty of the Khmer Rouge era. The museum serves multiple purposes: honoring the memory of victims, educating both Cambodians and international visitors about this genocide, and standing as a warning against the dangers of totalitarian ideology.

## Significance for Cambodia and the World

Tuol Sleng has become an essential site for understanding the Cambodian genocide, which claimed an estimated 1.7 to 2 million lives during the Khmer Rouge period. Alongside the Killing Fields of Choeung Ek, it forms part of a broader network of memorial sites that help Cambodia and the international community process this traumatic history.

The museum plays a crucial role in Cambodia's ongoing efforts toward reconciliation and healing. It also serves an important educational function, ensuring that future generations understand the consequences of extremist ideology and the importance of protecting human rights. For many survivors and families of victims, Tuol Sleng remains a place of remembrance and, in some cases, a path toward closure regarding the fate of loved ones who disappeared during this dark period.

Today, Tuol Sleng stands not only as a memorial to those who suffered but also as a testament to Cambodia's resilience and its commitment to ensuring that the atrocities of the past are never forgotten nor repeated.

# Khmer Rouge Prison Chief's Trial Resumes in Cambodia, Confronting Nation's Painful Past

**PHNOM PENH, Cambodia** — The war crimes tribunal for Kaing Guek Eav, the former Khmer Rouge prison chief known as "Duch," resumed this week at the U.N.-backed court on the outskirts of the capital, as survivors and relatives of victims packed the public gallery to witness a rare reckoning with one of the darkest chapters in Southeast Asian history.

Duch, 66, stands accused of overseeing the torture and execution of an estimated 15,000 men, women and children at Tuol Sleng, the notorious Phnom Penh detention center known as S-21, during the Khmer Rouge's brutal 1975-1979 rule. He faces charges of crimes against humanity, war crimes, murder and torture before the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia, a hybrid tribunal combining Cambodian and international law.

The proceedings, housed in a specially constructed courtroom capable of holding hundreds of spectators, opened this session with continued testimony examining the mechanics of the S-21 facility, where prisoners were systematically interrogated, tortured into false confessions, and later executed at the "Killing Fields" of Choeung Ek on the capital's outskirts.

## A Courtroom Weighted With Memory

Inside the chamber, the atmosphere remained solemn and tense. Elderly Cambodians, many wearing traditional white mourning scarves, sat alongside younger generations born after the regime's collapse, watching through a glass partition as proceedings unfolded. Simultaneous translation into Khmer, English and French crackled through headsets distributed to the gallery.

Duch himself, a former mathematics teacher who converted to evangelical Christianity in the 1990s, has adopted an unusual posture for a defendant facing such charges — at times expressing remorse and cooperating extensively with prosecutors, while his defense team has argued he was merely following orders from superiors in the regime's leadership, several of whom await separate trials.

"He says he is sorry, but sorry cannot bring back my family," said one survivor who lost several relatives during the period, speaking outside the courtroom during a recess. Many victims' relatives expressed mixed emotions — relieved that a legal process was finally underway more than three decades after the atrocities, yet frustrated by the tribunal's slow pace and limited scope.

## Documenting Atrocity

Prosecutors have relied heavily on the Khmer Rouge's own meticulous documentation — thousands of pages of forced confessions, prisoner logs and photographs that the regime itself compiled at S-21, inadvertently creating an extensive paper trail of its crimes. Expert witnesses have walked the court through this archive, corroborating testimony from the handful of known survivors of the facility.

Fewer than a dozen prisoners are believed to have survived S-21 out of the thousands who passed through its gates, and several of these survivors have provided harrowing testimony during the proceedings, describing torture techniques, starvation conditions and the climate of terror that pervaded the compound.

## A Test for Cambodian Justice

The tribunal, established through years of negotiation between the United Nations and the Cambodian government, has faced persistent criticism over funding shortfalls, allegations of political interference, and the slow pace of justice — Duch was first detained in 1999, nearly a decade before formal charges were filed.

Legal observers note the case carries significance beyond Duch's individual culpability, serving as a foundational test of whether the tribunal can deliver credible justice for the estimated 1.7 million Cambodians who died from execution, starvation, forced labor and disease during the Khmer Rouge's radical agrarian revolution.

Additional senior Khmer Rouge leaders, including former officials tied to the regime's inner circle, face separate forthcoming trials, though advancing age and health concerns among the aging defendants have raised questions about whether justice will arrive in time.

For now, the court has adjourned with further witness testimony expected in coming sessions, as Cambodia continues grappling with how to memorialize and prosecute atrocities that still shape the nation's collective memory a generation later.

*This report reflects proceedings as they occurred during the tribunal's active session; case developments continue to unfold.*

# Khmer Rouge Tribunal Delivers Verdict in Landmark S-21 Prison Case

**PHNOM PENH** — In a courtroom steeped in historical weight, the Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), a UN-backed tribunal, has issued a ruling in the case connected to the notorious S-21 detention facility, once again focusing global attention on one of the 20th century's most brutal regimes.

## The Killing Fields Legacy

Between 1975 and 1979, the Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, transformed Cambodia into a vast experiment in radical agrarian communism. Cities were emptied, currency abolished, and an estimated 1.7 to 2 million people—nearly a quarter of the population—perished through execution, starvation, and forced labor. The regime targeted intellectuals, ethnic minorities, religious figures, and perceived political enemies with systematic brutality.

At the center of this machinery of terror stood S-21, formerly Tuol Sleng High School in Phnom Penh, converted into the regime's principal interrogation and torture center. Of an estimated 12,000 to 20,000 people imprisoned there, only a handful are known to have survived. Detainees were photographed, forced into confessions under torture, and subsequently executed at the nearby Choeung Ek killing fields.

## The Long Road to Justice

The tribunal's origins trace back decades. Following the Khmer Rouge's fall from power in 1979, Cambodia endured years of civil conflict and political instability that delayed any reckoning with the past. It was not until 1997 that the Cambodian government requested UN assistance in establishing a tribunal, and further negotiations stretched until 2006 before the hybrid court—combining Cambodian and international judges and law—became operational.

The ECCC has faced persistent criticism over its slow pace, high costs exceeding hundreds of millions of dollars, and the deaths of several senior Khmer Rouge leaders, including Pol Pot himself in 1998, before facing justice. Kaing Guek Eav, known as "Duch," the commandant who ran S-21, became the tribunal's first convicted figure in 2010, sentenced to life imprisonment for crimes against humanity and war crimes.

## Significance for Survivors and History

For survivors and victims' families who packed the courtroom galleries, the proceedings carry profound emotional resonance. Many testified about lost relatives, torture, and the psychological scars that persist across generations. Cambodian civil society organizations have emphasized the tribunal's role in creating an official historical record, countering decades of denial and providing a legal framework acknowledging the atrocities.

"This tribunal cannot undo what happened," said one legal observer following proceedings, "but it establishes accountability where none existed, and it ensures the world cannot forget."

## Broader Implications

The case underscores enduring questions about transitional justice—how societies confront mass atrocity after the fact, often decades later. With aging defendants and witnesses, the tribunal races against time itself. Critics argue justice delayed represents justice incomplete, while supporters maintain that establishing truth, however late, serves victims and strengthens the rule of law in Cambodia.

As the ECCC's work draws toward its conclusion, its legacy will likely be judged not only by verdicts rendered but by its contribution to historical memory, reconciliation, and Cambodia's ongoing effort to reckon with the Khmer Rouge era's devastating legacy.

---

*This report reflects general historical background on the ECCC and Khmer Rouge tribunals. For current details on specific verdicts, sentencing, or ongoing proceedings, consult current wire services and official tribunal statements, as case specifics may have evolved.*

# Khmer Rouge Tribunal Resumes as Cambodia Confronts Its Darkest Chapter

PHNOM PENH — The Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC), the UN-backed tribunal established to prosecute senior leaders of the Khmer Rouge regime, has resumed proceedings this week, reigniting hopes among survivors and human rights advocates that justice may finally be served more than three decades after the fall of Pol Pot's brutal government.

The tribunal, a hybrid court combining Cambodian and international law and personnel, has faced years of delays, funding shortages, and allegations of political interference since its inception. Its mission remains monumental: to hold accountable the architects of a regime responsible for the deaths of an estimated 1.7 to 2 million Cambodians between 1975 and 1979 through executions, forced labor, starvation, and disease.

"This is about accountability, but it's also about memory," said Robert Petit, the tribunal's international co-prosecutor, in a statement addressing the court's resumed session. "We owe it to the victims, and to Cambodia's future generations, to ensure that this process is thorough, fair, and unflinching in its pursuit of the truth. The evidence is voluminous, the crimes are severe, and the world is watching to see whether international justice mechanisms can succeed even amid immense political and logistical challenges."

Petit acknowledged the difficulties that have plagued the court since its founding, including friction between international and Cambodian jurists over judicial independence, but expressed cautious optimism. "We are moving forward. That in itself is significant given the obstacles this tribunal has faced."

For many Cambodians, the tribunal's proceedings carry deep personal weight. Youk Chhang, director of the Documentation Center of Cambodia (DC-Cam), an organization that has spent decades gathering evidence and testimonies related to Khmer Rouge atrocities, emphasized the symbolic and educational significance of the trials.

"For years, survivors have waited—many have died waiting—to see even a measure of justice," Chhang said. "This tribunal is not just about punishing a few aging men; it is about giving voice to millions who suffered in silence. It's about teaching young Cambodians, who did not live through the Khmer Rouge era, what happened here so that history does not repeat itself."

Chhang, whose organization has provided critical documentation used as evidence in the proceedings, noted that public engagement with the tribunal has been essential to its legitimacy. "We have brought thousands of Cambodians from the countryside to observe these hearings. For many, it is the first time they have seen the men responsible for their suffering face any form of judicial scrutiny. That alone has value, regardless of the ultimate verdicts."

The tribunal has been dogged by criticism over its slow pace and high costs, with proceedings costing tens of millions of dollars annually, funded largely by international donors including Japan, Australia, and various European nations. Critics have also raised concerns about the advanced age and declining health of several defendants, raising fears that some may die before verdicts are reached—a concern already realized with the death of certain indicted figures during earlier proceedings.

Despite these challenges, officials maintain that the tribunal represents a crucial, if imperfect, mechanism for addressing historical atrocities. Human rights organizations have pointed to the ECCC as a potential model—albeit a flawed one—for hybrid tribunals in other post-conflict societies grappling with mass atrocity accountability.

As proceedings continue, survivors, scholars, and international observers alike will be watching closely to see whether the tribunal can deliver meaningful justice, or whether it will be remembered primarily as a cautionary tale about the limits of international legal intervention decades after the fact.

For Cambodia, a nation still healing from one of the twentieth century's most devastating genocides, the stakes—both symbolic and substantive—could not be higher.

PHNOM PENH — Proceedings continue at the UN-backed Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC) in the case against Kaing Guek Eav, better known as "Duch," the former commandant of the notorious S-21 prison, known today as Tuol Sleng.

**Background on the Case**

Duch, now elderly, faced charges including crimes against humanity, grave breaches of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, and torture stemming from his role overseeing the S-21 facility between 1975 and 1979, during the Khmer Rouge regime under Pol Pot.

**Key Facts About S-21:**

- Historians estimate between 12,000 and 20,000 people passed through S-21
- Documented survivors from the facility are believed to number fewer than a dozen
- The facility was formerly Tuol Svay Prey High School before its conversion into a prison and interrogation center
- Extensive documentation, including photographs of prisoners, was maintained by the regime itself

**Testimony and Trial Elements**

The tribunal has heard from survivors, former S-21 staff, and relatives of victims. Testimony has included accounts from individuals who survived due to specialized skills the regime found useful, as well as former guards describing the internal hierarchy and procedures at the facility.

Duch himself offered testimony acknowledging command responsibility for the facility while providing varying accounts regarding the extent of his personal actions.
